theme: The Book of the Covenant, case laws
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 21:1-22:31. These two chapters contain the first set of laws that follow the Ten Commandments. They can feel foreign and sometimes hard. Read them slowly, and ask what each law shows about God’s concern for justice, for the vulnerable, and for human life.
settingTheScene: After the Ten Commandments, God gives Moses a long set of specific rulings called the Book of the Covenant (Exodus 20:22-23:33). They are case laws, applications of the broad principles of the Ten Commandments to the daily life of an agricultural society in the ancient Near East. This is not the part of the Bible that most new readers enjoy. But it is worth reading carefully, because it shows how God cares about the details of everyday justice. The laws also come to us in a particular covenant with Israel at a particular time, and reading them well means knowing how they fit the whole story.
observation: The first law concerns Hebrew servants: “When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing” (21:2).
Kidnapping is a capital crime: “Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death” (21:16).
Laws on injury include the principle, “You shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot” (21:23-24).
If a slave is injured by a master, the slave is to go free (21:26-27).
If an ox gores someone, the owner is held responsible if he knew it was dangerous (21:28-36).
Laws on theft and restitution require thieves to repay several times over (22:1-4).
“You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (22:21).
“You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. If you do afflict them…my wrath will burn” (22:22-24).
“If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you, you shall not be to him as a moneylender, and you shall not exact interest from him” (22:25).
“If ever you take your neighbor’s cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down…for when he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate” (22:26-27).
interpretation:
The first thing to understand is the way these laws are written. They are case laws: “If a man does this, then this is the consequence.” They are not an exhaustive legal code. They are examples that train judges to think about justice. The laws are also specific to the setting of ancient Israel. Modern readers sometimes want to treat every verse as a rule for today, or else dismiss the whole thing as irrelevant. Neither is right. The better approach is to ask what each law reveals about God’s character, and how the principle is fulfilled in Christ.

Take the opening law about servants. It may trouble modern readers, and the questions are fair. Slavery is a hard subject, and the Bible does not hide from it. But look at what the law actually does. The servitude it describes is a form of debt labor, limited to six years, with release in the seventh. Kidnapping and selling a person is punished by death. Injury to a slave sets the slave free. In a world where slaves were property without rights, the law gives human beings dignity and protection. It does not describe the ideal. It restrains the worst. The deeper message, “You were sojourners in Egypt,” appeals to the exodus. Israel is to remember that they were slaves once, and that the LORD set them free.

The “eye for eye” principle is easy to misread. In its original setting, it is a limit, not a license for revenge. The punishment must fit the crime and go no further. This protects against escalating retaliation. Jesus will take the principle deeper in Matthew 5:38-39, telling his followers to renounce personal revenge: “If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.” He is not abolishing the court’s duty to do justice. He is calling individuals to a higher way of living.

The most striking pattern in these chapters is the care for the weak. The sojourner, the widow, the orphan, and the poor borrower are all named. God says that when they cry out, “I will surely hear their cry” (22:23). The God who heard the cry of Israel in Egypt now commands Israel to hear the cry of the vulnerable. His justice is shaped by his own experience of redeeming slaves. The cloak law is a gem: a poor man’s coat, taken as a pledge, must be returned by nightfall, because he needs it to sleep in. And the reason given is simply: “for I am compassionate.”

Paul shows how to read these laws in light of Christ in 1 Corinthians 9:9-10. He quotes the law, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” and applies it to paying ministers. He sees in the law a principle of fairness that goes beyond the particular case. We are to read the case laws as windows into the heart of God.
connection: Jesus said that the greatest in the kingdom would be the servant of all (Mark 10:43-45). Paul’s letter to Philemon asks a master to receive his runaway slave “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). James 1:27 says that “religion that is pure and undefiled before God” is “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction.” Leviticus 19:33-34 repeats the command to love the sojourner.
application:
Read the laws on the vulnerable in 22:21-27 again. Who are the sojourners, widows, orphans, and poor borrowers in your community? Choose one action this week to help one of them.

Practice reading hard passages by asking what they reveal about God’s character. Write down one thing you learn about God from today’s reading.

Thank God that he is compassionate, and let that shape the way you treat people who owe you something.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you his heart for the stranger, the widow, and the orphan.
Ask him for humility as you read his law.
Tell him where you are asking Christ to show you more.
